extracted.intended_audience: 3D artists, illustrators, and science communicators (especially those using Sketchfab)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating interactive 3D visuals on Sketchfab to illustrate scientific and mathematical ideas, emphasizing storytelling, interaction, and practical constraints of the platform. Focuses on decisions about medium, technique, annotation, and experimentation to make conceptual research accessible and engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell a story / spark interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal is not necessarily to make realistic representations but to tell a story and spark interest; 'If a visual can communicate the essence of a concept well enough that someone can internalize and own it, all the better.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer visuals that communicate the essence of theoretical or invisible concepts (quantum processes, higher-dimensional geometries, time). Prioritize narrative clarity and viewer understanding over photorealism. Use visual metaphors or procedures that let viewers grasp a conceptual kernel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use immersive interaction to invite discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketchfab's strength lies in tapping into the desire for immersive interaction—the site 'strips away all the AI trying to kill you and leaves the exploration.' Interaction invites active participation and discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design models that encourage rotation, panning, and exploration so viewers participate mentally by 'filling in the blanks.' Consider techniques (diorama, hidden geometry) that reward exploration with revelations tied to the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the right medium for the job
rubrics_metrics.description: If we’re talking about a 3D object, why not show it in 3D? Sometimes it’s just about using the best medium for the job.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether 3D is actually necessary; when it is, embed interactive models rather than static images. Consider audience/device compatibility and the affordances of 3D vs. video/2D.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer light, cross-device embeds
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketchfab embeds are so light (a lossless interactive model can be smaller than a compressed video, or even the same size as a high-res JPG) and work well across devices—there’s no drawback to these engaging 'educational toys.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor formats and optimizations that keep file size small for fast loading and cross-device performance. Use Sketchfab where embedding an interactive model is more efficient than video or many static images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotations are crucial for usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to add annotations (with links and even images) is crucial for making these models useful for readers; they’re one of the reasons I chose Sketchfab over similar viewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use annotations to direct attention, explain parts of the model, link to related articles, or add images—rather than leaving viewers to guess. For explanatory models (e.g., Standard Model of Particle Physics, Mars landing sites), annotate salient features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work within platform animation constraints creatively
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketchfab-readable animations can only scale, move, or rotate. Or they have to be alembics (kind of like a flip-book, if each page was a file—these can get heavy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When complex animations are desired, break the effect into parts and stitch them together (e.g., unraveling by scaling sequential parts). Favor simple transformations (scale/move/rotate) and plan around alembic file-size tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Model Inspector to learn and reproduce clever methods
rubrics_metrics.description: My favorite Sketchfab tool is probably the Model Inspector. Using the Inspector, I love discovering all the clever methods other artists employ to create illusions and stretch the limitations of these tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect others' models to see how illusions are achieved; reverse-engineer techniques to inform your own solutions. This learning-by-inspection approach fuels experimentation and better craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ illusion and stylistic choices to evoke surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques like lack of lighting and flat textures can make 3D models look like 2D images at first, creating a feeling of surprise—'It’s like walking into a painting.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deliberate stylistic constraints (flat textures, limited lighting, woodcut-like styles, diorama framing) to mimic feelings associated with scientific discovery or to emphasize conceptual aspects. Surprise can increase engagement and memorability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simplified, abstracted models as effective samples/mocks
rubrics_metrics.description: Models are often used as a kind of 'sample' or 'mock-up,' simplified and abstracted from context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t feel obligated to model full contextual complexity; abstractions can highlight the phenomenon of interest. Simplify geometry and visuals to focus viewer attention on the conceptual point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance risk of interaction-driven payoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving a viewer the opportunity to make a discovery for themselves is risky (because we can’t ensure interaction or payoff), but it can be a meaningful narrative device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design interactive discoveries knowing some users won’t interact; provide enough cues or annotations to reward exploration but avoid making the message dependent solely on user action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment and publish personal tests
rubrics_metrics.description: I like to experiment with Sketchfab’s capabilities, and sometimes publish those to my personal account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the platform as a sandbox: prototype ideas, try simple solutions, and publish experiments to learn what works. Use personal uploads to iterate before institutional publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross disciplinary collaboration and medium-mixing
rubrics_metrics.description: Going forward, I’d love to collaborate more with other 3D artists to realize wonderful, unconventional ideas, or just make cool models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine 3D with 2D art, narrative writing, or other media. Break conventions and use cross-boundary ideas to find new ways to illustrate scientific concepts.
